utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. File, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pasalic -- Professor Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: When we left off yesterday I was asking you about page 39 in the English and page 37 in the B/C/S of your report and how you came up with the distribution of ethnic groups in table 3. You pointed me to table 2, which has a breakdown of population by age and sex but not ethnicity, and then you explained to me that you used a differentiated birth rate formula to generate those figures but you could not specify a paragraph in the report that showed those calculations. Now, I want to go to the next page of your report and show you a place where a similar thing happened. This is in paragraph 115. We have some figures from table B2.2 of P4994 which was Dr. Tabeau's report, and then you add a column that says "Should be" with different percentages. Now, you have a footnote there that just says that the data is taken from your own scientific book, but there's no explanation as to how you arrived at those figures; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain that table. The figures are correct, and they show the difference between the results of Dr. Tabeau and mine. This table follows from the previous misstated data and from table 2, the age structure of the population. With these figures we have shown that those born until 1980 in Dr. Tabeau's report and in my report differ in numbers. The column should be -- is based on the calculation of these variables of age structure and the differentiated birth rate as well as natural population growth which shows that in the Serbian population --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Professor, once again I'm just looking for the calculations. I'm looking for where these numbers come from. I understand that you're using different variables that produce it, but I'm wondering how can anyone try to replicate these numbers if you don't show them how you're doing the calculations.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The calculation is very simple and can be found in other paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Which paragraph? Can you point me to the paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I would ask for a little patience. Paragraph 92 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. File kindly speak into the other microphone as well please or switch on both microphones. We can hardly hear him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the table, the variable of population growth by ethnicity. If you apply this variable in your calculation, then you easily arrive at the result that the Serbian population is more numerous in the age group born until 1980, but the population growth is half that of the Muslim population, and then we get these results which differ from those of Dr. Tabeau, because the share of the Serbs until 1980 relatively speaking is much greater than -- than according to her calculations in which she used her methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm sure --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are all original data from vital statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. But I'm sure you see the problem which is that here you have percentages but there is no calculation anywhere. That's point. There's no indication of your methodology.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may. I can show that in the example given in paragraph 110 after table 2. I show a calculation applied to the example of one municipality. All other calculations are done along the same lines, because the same variables and the same formula are used. In such analyses, it is unnecessary to burden the report with calculations and mathematical statistical formulae. It is important to present the results parallelly to those of the OTP's expert and point out the differences, and the differences are obvious. I stand by the accuracy of my data. I think that there is no doubt about the accuracy, but we -- you must apply demography and statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Again, I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, the transcript -- in line 8, the word "vital statistics" is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: To be clear, Professor, the calculation that you did in paragraph 110, which you're relying on now, is a calculation that produces in point 4 the total population born before 1980, and that's the total population of 3.523.437. And I'm asking you how you produced a figure that has a breakdown of internally displaced persons between Serbs, Muslims, Croats, and others, and you have percentages. There's literally no connection between a calculation that produces a complete population for a country and a calculation that produces percentages of internally displaced persons broken down by ethnicity. They're not related, are they?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both have to do with paragraph 92. I gave per mils percentages that I apply in table B22 in the calculation of percentages allocating the share of Serbs, Muslims, and the refugee population. I thereby show that the data for vital statistics must be used and namely the differentiated vital population growth. That is an essential variable that the OTP expert did for the take into consideration and this is the greatest difference between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you about the next table, which is table 4 on page 41 of the English and page 38 to 39 of the B/C/S. Now, the source for this is an RS government list of refugees and displaced persons in Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Table 4 is presented on the basis of a primary data source, and that is the comprehensive census of displaced persons and refugees which was taken immediately after the war in the most important year, and that year is 1996. If you want me to explain this table.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Not at the moment. I'm going to ask you some questions about the table, actually. It covers exclusively the territory of Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This table covers the territory of Republika Srpska, but there were persons from all over Bosnia-Herzegovina and also from without Bosnia-Herzegovina, persons who came to the territory of the RS, which shows their intensive demographic movements in all directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So just to compare this with the Tabeau report, this misses some of the municipalities that are covered by the Tabeau report, and it also includes some that are not included in the Tabeau report, is that right, in terms of the overlap?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an aggregate report for refugees and displaced persons who came to the RS. In other tables which we can also look at, we deal with municipalities that Dr. Tabeau also dealt with --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm not asking about other tables.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that's what we can compare.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about other tables, I'm asking about this table. Are these all Serbs that are included within this table?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We will see that later --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- when we come to the structure of the refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It cannot be seen in this table but they're dominant.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And these are all people who arrived in Republika Srpska, not people who fled the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my reports, I don't know if the annex was admitted. There were both people who came to the RS and those who left the RS. These are migration flows and counter flows. But this table shows the overall process, and it was not necessary to show some data about refugees and displaced persons based on some samples. She didn't use that primary source. And in some other tables we show from where these other persons came to the RS. I repeat that this is a primary data source, and it is extremely valid as compared to secondary data sources which we used by Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could you please just answer my question directly. I asked you whether this table covers people who arrived in RS exclusively but not people who fled the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case this table covers all the persons -- all the persons who came to the territory of the RS from other -- some other territories. It is clearly stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. So don't you see a problem then in terms of methodology here in the sense that you're using numbers that can't be compared to the data in the Tabeau report because she's talking about people who fled some but not all of the territories that are covered in this table and other territories that are not covered in this table? There are multiple ways that this doesn't interact with the data in Dr. Tabeau's report; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the essence, indeed, to show the whole process, but that is missing in Dr. Tabeau's report. She only shows migration flows in one direction, and we show the other direction. So we can show the totality of the process in both directions, and that is the essence of demographic movements during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We cannot understand any process -- or, rather, we will have a distorted picture or wrong statistics if we only look at one aspect of the process without taking into consideration the causes and consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you about a calculation question or issue which is earlier in your report. It appears on page 31 of the English and 28 of the B/C/S. It's at paragraph 85. You're claiming that in the addendum to the Tabeau report she made errors of calculation when determining the number of people born before 1980 in order to look for matches of eligible registered voters in OSCE voting register for 1997, and in paragraph 85 you say that her figures are "not real" and that this can be easily proven using Bijeljina as an example. In paragraphs 85 to 86, you explain that Dr. Tabeau listed the number of Bijeljina inhabitants before -- born before 1980 as totaling 81.650 in 1991, and you say that because the 1991 census shows the total population of Bijeljina as 96.988, the consequences that Dr. Tabeau's numbers would show 84.18 per cent of the population born before 1980, and presumably this is because if you divide 81.650 by the total population of 96.988, you get 84.18 per cent. And then you describe this result in paragraph 86 as absolutely incorrect, and you say, and now I'm quoting your report: "According to the age structure in Bijeljina in 1991, Bijeljina 25.584 residents younger than 18 or 26.37 per cent. This is irrefutable proof that it is impossible for Bijeljina to have had only 15.82 per cent of inhabitants aged less than 18, the share given by international experts in annex A1. Such sudden changes in age structure are not possible in only seven or eight years. Likewise, the data on the population of all ethnicities, including the Muslims, as presented in annex A1 for all presented municipalities was also done in an erroneous and incorrect way." Now, have I accurately described your objection to Dr. Tabeau's calculations there?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You interpreted everything based on these two paragraphs. These two are the ones where constitute the most striking proof that Dr. Tabeau calculated wrongly on the very simple example that at Bijeljina municipality we showed that -- that there is a huge difference in the population born before 1980, and I will show gladly how we arrived at these figures, and by inference also the data for all the other municipalities are wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So let's go to the next page of your report, which is paragraph 91. You reiterate this point using a chart of the age distribution of the population of Bijeljina in 1991, and you say at the bottom of the page: "The table shows that the estimates given by the international experts were exaggerated and may not be taken as relevant data for production of evidence in any significant case that treats such demographic issues." So what I want to do with you now is just to do a sort of back of the envelope calculation with you using your own table that we see here to approximate the percentage of the population that was born before 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So if we could switch to Sanction for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Can you see there your table from paragraph 91 which shows the age distribution of the population of Bijeljina according to 1991 census data?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: The left-hand side column shows the age group and the right-hand side column shows the number of individuals who were included in that age group; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So if you want to figure out from this approximately how many people were born in 1980 or after, and this data comes from 1991, then you're essentially looking for people who are between the ages of 0 and 11; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first two categories 0 through 9 and 10 through 14, everyone is included. Yes, until the age of 11, you're right. And in the second category we consider half of the population relevant as those born until 1980, because if we were to consider the whole age group it would consider those born after 1980 as well. We calculate that based on the differentiated natural population growth.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, strictly speaking it's not half. It's 40 per cent, right, because the ages are 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14, so there are five year groups and we're looking for 10-year-olds and 11-year-olds?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two and a half and two and a half. The interval is five here. In statistical tables these are nominal limits, and these intervals are the calculated as the upper limit of the previous group minus the lower limit of the previous group.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it's done in statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. So if you -- if you want to produce this number, you start by pulling out all the people who are 0 to 9 years old, and we can actually go to the next -- there we go. You pull out that number first, and then you select out the 10-year-olds and the 11-year-olds. If we go to the next slide. And the next one. You select that group of people to include the total population, if we're approximating, of 0 to 11; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 0, 11, and half of 12 in that year. We make an estimate of age 12 and divide -- and split it in two, two equal parts, if we want the period up until 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: But actually wouldn't you also be splitting the age 9 into two parts? So as a result, the total would be 0 to 9 plus age 10 and 11; right? Not half. It's two fits.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no need for 9. This is the whole contingent of those born after 1980; that is, minors. There is no need to split them. The problem is the group from 10 to 14 years. Some were born before 1980, others after 1980. This is where you have to calculate and apply estimates to establish how many were born before 1980 and how many later.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And I apologise to the registrar for switching back to e-court for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: The reason this is surprising to me is I'm using your own methodology for doing this kind of calculation from page 34 of your report where you actually do this for Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So could we just look at -- it's the top of page 34 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And do you see what I'm saying? It says at the top the age structure of the population of Prijedor in 1991, and you've got the same categories that you have listed for Bijeljina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's find -- yes. We see the B/C/S. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And then in the paragraph afterwards it says: "Therefore, if we take away all the residents in the 0-9 age group and the relevant proportion in the 10-14 age group," and then in parentheses you have two-fifths. You don't have one-half, you have two-fifths. Now do you see how that's different from what you're just telling me?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm following.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So shall we return to the calculation that we were doing before using your own methodology here.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two-fifths apply to age 10 and 11. This does not yet include the half of the 12-year-olds, because the total size is 5, that is the interval, plus age group 10, 11, 12, 13, 14. We take two-fifths, which is 10 and 11, and then we estimate one-half of age 12. The methodology is completely the same for Bijeljina, Prijedor, and any other municipality. It only differs from the variable based on differentiated natural population growth and that's why we get different percentages.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: But that's not what you do in your report. In your report, you take two-fifths of the 10 to 14 age group. If you do the math, that's what that is. That's two-fifths. And then you say we get to the result that in 1991, and then you have a simple subtraction from the total population from the group of 0 to 9-year-olds and then the 10 and 11-year-olds. There's nothing there about taking half of the 12-year-olds and adding them to this number. I'm sorry to focus on the details, but that's not what you put in the report.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only possibility that I see is that this was skipped while in the printing, that it was omitted, but it's impossible that it had not been taken into account in the calculations when you look at the final results which you have at the end of paragraph 93.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Professor, how was it skipped in the printing when you actually you do the numbers? You subtract 19.667 from 112.543 and you arrive at 98276 for Prijedor. That's not a printing error.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is. I think that it was most probably omitted. However, even if we were to include here half of year 12, the result would be even more -- would prove even more my point for this calculation. The data here is somewhat less than it should be, but the methodology is -- points out the difference between what we used, the method that we used, and Dr. Tabeau, her methodology also on the example of Prijedor. If you look further at the differentiated birth rate, you will see the percentages that show that there was a far greater share of the Muslim population born after 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm not asking --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other words, their numbers of the -- of those born before 1980 were smaller, lower, objectively than Dr. Tabeau presented it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: All right. Let's return to this calculation relating to Bijeljina, and we're going to do it the way that you did it in your report, and then we can make an adjustment afterwards for this half of the 12-year-olds.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That shows the addition of these two groups which adds up to 16.184.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now if you do a percentage this way, what you produce is a number that is 16.68 per cent of age 0 to 11, which is people born 1980 or later, and then 83.32 per cent of people aged 12 or over, i.e., born before 1980. Now, this -- first of all, this is an approximation because we're taking an evenly distributed assumption of every age group, and it's probably not precisely that way. So this will be different from Dr. Tabeau's figures probably somewhat because she counted individual people, but these figures are awfully close. Dr. Tabeau said 84.18 per cent, and we have 83.32 per cent. Now, even if you were to add half of the age 12-year-olds, we can even -- we can do this calculation, actually. You have to add 666 people to 16.184, which gives 16.850, and then you divide by 96.988, and you end up with 17.37 per cent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: An older group being 82.6 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So again, even if we follow this methodology that you're telling us about today that's different from what you had in your report, you still get a number that's quite close to the number that Dr. Tabeau produced. Now, let's revisit for a moment your criticism, because you said in paragraph 86: "According to the age structure in 1991, Bijeljina had 25.584 residents younger than 18 or 26.37 per cent." But the point is, Professor, Dr. Tabeau wasn't interested in people who became voting age in 1991. She was interested in the people who became voting age in 1997 because those were the people who were going to show up in the 1997 voters register. So it doesn't matter what percentage of residents were younger than 18 in 1991. What matters is what percentage of residents were younger than 12 in 1991. So my question is that when you claim that Dr. Tabeau has made a mistake that infects all the municipality's figures in her annex A1, it's actually you who've made the mistake, and this is a pretty fundamental mistake, isn't it, for a demographer? To use the word that you used yesterday, this is kind of an amateurish mistake, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And I claim with absolute certainty and please let me prove this. It is correct that Dr. Tabeau used the matching method where she matched the information from the census of 1991, those who were born before 1980, and the voters' registers of 1997 in order to show that in 1998 those who had the right to vote. In other words, who were of mature age. Now, our methodology shows that it is impossible that between 1991 and 1997 for this population to have grown old so fast and that we get 84.18 per cent of those who had the right to vote in 1997 and 1998. Those were -- these were the oldest populations in some countries of Europe. Let me remind you of this, that in 1991, the average age in Bosnia and Herzegovina was 33, which in percentage points means that about 75 of the grown-ups had the right to vote. It is impossible to have this transformation from 75 per cent that I've calculated here to 84 per cent of those who were born before 1980 and who have the right to vote by 1997, because this would be a very sudden aging of the population, and this is where we show the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have the final slide of this in e-court as 65 ter number 24766, and I would tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How do we view that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I think if we switch to e-court it should come up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. 24766. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6198, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure Doctor has understood your question, last question, whether Dr. Tabeau was interested in the percentage of voting people in the year of 1991. So she didn't pay any attention to those who were 12 to 18 in 1991, did she?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes. The people -- she did. The people who were 12 to 18 in 1991 are voting age in 1997. So it's only the 0 to 11-year-olds that we're concerned with excluding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I misspoke. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm actually going to move to table 12 unless Your Honours think that I should pursue this further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me -- bear with me a minute. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I want to look at this large table that you have, table 12, that runs from English page 46 to 53 and B/C/S page 43 to 50. Now, this table purports to show the number of households who moved into various municipalities in Republika Srpska as measured in 1996, and it shows the number of households that moved in from other municipalities and regions; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, the number of households.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And some of these are indictment municipalities and some of them are not; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The table shows the municipalities with migrating populations, the populations that arrived into the municipality. From the case of Mr. Karadzic, we just wanted to show by some data, comparative data, that those municipalities are not representatives and that the indictment municipalities are not -- that the demographic movements in those municipalities are not so expressive as we would say in demography and demographic analysis. We will show that later. So the 20 Karadzic indictment municipalities. Should we explain the table?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I explain it, because it's a bit complicated?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions about it, but I'm just wondering you also included some municipalities that are not in the indictment; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This table did not include the municipalities where people from other municipalities came except from the municipalities in the Karadzic case, because our goal was to show the difference between our results and the OTP expert's results.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that the figures are far lower than shown in those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I don't think you're answering my question, but --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I propose that we show at least one version. Because these are figures, we don't really need to have translation into English. Could we just show the table and perhaps zoom in on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a question about what -- what data this -- this table provides. It does not provide data on ethnicity; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, no, because these are demographic movements of members of all ethnicities in larger and smaller percentages.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So then this is what I don't understand, is in your report at paragraph 130, which is page 43 of the B/C/S, you say: "The relative decrease in the proportion of one ethnic group in the general population may be due to the departure of its members but also to the arrival of another ethnic group." But this data that you're using doesn't show the arrival of another ethnic group. It shows the arrival of households, period. Ethnic group is not a variable that's measured here; right? Actually, you've already answered that question. Let me show you where you do this again after table 12. It's paragraph 132. You say: "Let us have a look at the influx of Serbian families to the 20 municipalities in the Karadzic case." And then for the next page and a half you use the same data to look at three of the 20 municipalities, and again you're using data with no information about ethnicity and you're claiming that you're proving something related to the movement of ethnic groups. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, these are data from the census, so I was not the one who created them. They were given without the ethnicity category. They were given in total numbers. But the essence of these tables is what I say in paragraph 132 where we show that in Banja Luka, in the Dr. Karadzic case, only 22.5 per cent of people arrived from the -- from the municipalities that his case is concerned with and not all 100 per cent. So we show that this sample of municipalities is not representative and that in fact the data is exaggerated. Now, if we were to analyse --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... the key -- the key thing is --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that these are predominantly Serbian households that gravitated from other areas towards Republika Srpska, and we refer to this as the principle of connected vessels, and this applied to all ethnicities. You cannot take this in isolation, because one change would automatically cause a change in the other group. These are living individuals, they are human beings, and we show that these movements are very complex. That's what we're pointing out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You're saying that they're predominantly Serb, but there is no way you can give us a figure because you don't know. This data doesn't tell you. So we just have to take your word for it and assume that it's a lot but we don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that sense you could say so, but I don't have the right to change the data source because that's what I'm referring to here. This is a census of refugees and displaced persons. Anything other would be just my arbitrary estimation or assessments that are not valid, and I was very careful to stay away from that. In other words, I tried to corroborate, support every data with primary source data -- data source.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to switch gears and ask you about your criticisms of the 1991 census as a source. You say in your report and you also testified yesterday that the census reports were not verified, that the process data was never published, and you complain third of all that the results were published in 1995 in Croatia. I'd like to start with that last critique. At paragraph 57, this is page 25 of the English and page 24 of the B/C/S, regarding the fact that the 1991 census results were published in Croatia in 1995, you say: "... it is unusual and even absurd that a serious study should be based on census results of one country that were published in another maybe even more biased country." Now, first of all, what do you mean when you call Croatia an even more biased country?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's only a hypothetical assumption that there might be bias there, because in wartime another state is publishing in part the results of a census in another country, which is totally absurd. You can't find a similar example anywhere else in the world. The state bureau of statistics in Croatia published part of the data from the census in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1995 that relates to the entire population. Now, from the aggregate level, meaning the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina, all the way down to the towns and places, and that's why we said this was totally absurd. In scientific circles, that's unheard of. It was a surprise to us. And we challenge this information because this was never ratified by the then the National Assembly in Bosnia-Herzegovina which is a must, and this I corroborate by quoting someone who was an official of the bureau of statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Can we please look at 65 ter number 242L, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: What you will see on your screen in a moment, Professor, is the 1991 census results that were published in 1995 in Croatia. I'm going to show you a page with statistics for Vlasenica. I just chose this because I used it with another witness relatively recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This will be at e-court page 2 in the B/C/S. And if we can zoom in on Vlasenica. Maybe we should just make the B/C/S full screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In this what you have -- you have a total 1991 population of 33.942 in Vlasenica. Then you have Croats, 39; Muslims, 18.272; Serbs, 14.359; Yugoslavs, 340; and others, 477. Okay? Now, I want to compare that with 65 ter number 12121A.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could do that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And what you will see here when it comes up are the 1991 census results published in Sarajevo for Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And for the record, the .mif information indicates that this was seized by the OTP from the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo on 15 September 1994. Now, if we could go to e-court B/C/S page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You will see Vlasenica in the middle, and here you see the same numbers, 33.942 for the total population -- I'm not going to read them all, but they're the same. The only difference is they don't have a percentage, and the ethnicities are listed in a different order. That's the only difference. Otherwise, these are identical. Don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did not challenge the difference in the figures. What we see on the screen now are the first results that were published by the Bureau of Statistics of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the raw, the first results, not final. This shows the number of inhabitants but not the national -- but not the breakdown by ethnicity. This was only later published by the State bureau of Statistics of Croatia, but there is a third source, the federal bureau of statistics, which provided a detailed analysis. It is possible that in some municipalities there are certain differences in the figures because - I repeat - these were the initial results from Bosnia-Herzegovina that were not further analysed and published, but I have to say that it is strange that a census would be published by one state for another state under these conditions. So that is our main objection, not looking at every figure and so on. These are not relevant matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: But if the numbers are the same, then what does it matter where it was published? How can bias enter into the question if the numbers are the same?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's nonsense. You say that one state would not publish its census. We, too, used that information, that data, because we didn't have anything better, so we used the data from the State Bureau of Statistics of Croatia for the same figures, but it is indicative that during the war another state would publish your results, the results of your census. We could also ask why it wouldn't have been published by another state, by Serbia or Republika Srpska and so on. We did not go into challenging all of these figures. We didn't do that. But I apologise. I have to say these are just partially published results, not full results. Just total numbers and ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we tender these please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We'll admit them both.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6199 and P6200, respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Let's talk about this objection that you're raising now. You mention it in your report as well at paragraph 58. This is page 25 to 26 of the English and page 24 of the B/C/S. Now, here you pull out this quotation from Nora Selimovic's detailed description of the procedure followed. She was the expert advisor for aggregation and analysis of data and the development of the methodology in the field of demography in the BH agency for statistics in Sarajevo. Now this is in the Tabeau report, and she says -- you pull this quotation where she says: "The bureau of statistics was not able to produce and publish all tables that had to be prepared according to the programme of data processing. After the end of the military conflict, the statistical office managed to publish some more data in connection with the population and households. The data on dwellings and agricultural farms were not published because this material never passed the phase of logical control." Now in your report at paragraph 59, you go on to say: "Therefore our thesis on incomplete data from the 1991 BH census is fully confirmed by this quote." And this is the point you were just making. But if we look at P4993, which is the annex, Annex B of sources, you omit to mention that three paragraphs later in that exact same passage Nora Selimovic says: "The official data published on the population has passed all control phases including the control for duplicates that was conducted on the level of each municipality. So I put it to you, Professor, that what you're doing here is misrepresenting what's in the Tabeau report. You're making sweeping claims about how the census data is incomplete and unreliable, but you're basing it on the fact that some data about dwellings and farms was never published because it had not passed through some controls, whereas the rest of the data had been fully checked. That's what you're doing here in your report; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And by the way the citation for Tabeau quotation is e-court page 17, B/C/S page 15, and it's written on the page as page 206 because it came from the Milosevic report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: But that is what you're doing, right, Professor? You're misrepresenting what was in the Tabeau report.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. No. Please, paragraph 58 is Selimovic's quote, not mine. "Information regarding residents and any land in the person's possession, that was never published because that was never logically checked." Those are not my words. It's merely a quote that I'm using to demonstrate the incomplete nature of data used for the 1991 census. It's been 20 years and we still don't have all the information from that census processed. We have the initial results from the 1991 census, and we have the Annual Gazette of the bureau from 1998 which only tells us about the age groups but that is all we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So can I then ask you about --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my allegations, every inch of the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just pause -- bear in mind our conversation is being translated. You should put a pause. Shall we see the actual word in P4993, the passage you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As I was saying, it's -- it's in e-court page 17 of P4993. Oh, sorry. It's actually -- yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: The relevant passage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about the B/C/S page?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I actually don't have that. Oh, no, I do. It's page 15. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: What you can see here is the quotation that Professor Pasalic is referring to is that which occurs just above "concept de jure." And actually it starts on the previous page in the English. And then at the bottom of that section with concept de jure, you have the subsequent explanation by the census official explaining how official data on the population had passed all control phases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do we find that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It's the third paragraph below "concept de jure." It's a one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "The official data published on the population --"

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "-- has passed all control phases including the control for duplicate that was conducted on the level of each municipality." The question was whether Dr. Pasalic took this paragraph in consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That's the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Doctor. Yes, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can tell, we're looking at people who are temporarily employed outside Bosnia and Herzegovina. We're talking about the control stage including the illumination of duplicates. So this is the match -- matching method used by Dr. Tabeau, and we're not talking about complete data from the 1991 census. So there's something I'm unsure about as to how the two were actually linked together. We're talking about de jure and de facto. These are two concepts that are applied in a census. What does de jure mean? That concept means that all the population there physically present in Bosnia-Herzegovina is registered as long as they've been there for at least a year, which means in actual fact that everybody found in the territory is registered. So I'm talking about this in order to drive the point home about persons temporarily living and working abroad outside Bosnia-Herzegovina. But I don't think that all of this has to do with the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: None of that -- none of that is -- is mentioned there. It just says that official data published on the population has passed all control phases. It doesn't say only matching or only control for duplicates. It says all control phases. And at the top, that's where it talks about agricultural farms and dwellings that were not published because it hasn't passed a phase of logical control. So there's a pretty clear distinction there, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As soon as we're talking about duplicates, the reference is to the matching method used by Dr. Tabeau. We don't have that method and we make no reference to it. The previous quote is clearly -- the previous passage is quote by Nora Selimovic saying that the control phase was not taken into account when the census information was processed and analyzed. Each census goes through a number of different stages, data collection, data grouping, data analysis, and the eventual publication. This process never completed in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move on to a different subject because we're a little bit limited on time. Dr. -- Dr. Tabeau used a statistical technique to estimate the number of killed in Sarajevo called capture-recapture or multiple system estimation. Now on the 26th of April 2012, when Dr. Tabeau was testifying, Dr. Karadzic challenged the validity of capture-recapture technique, this is at transcript page 28188, and Trial Chamber noted after he said: "I challenge the formula, but if you do so it will be noted that your expert is challenging this formula itself." And I would note that you were physically present in the courtroom that day. Now, from your report at paragraph 47, you call this technique "the imaginary formula." So I need to ask you, do you dispute the validity of this formula?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then as now, I do. Why? It's a mathematical and statistical formula which does not, not by a long shot, give a realistic result of the phenomena being studied here. We have shown here on a number of occasions that Dr. Tabeau was to all practical intents using a non-existent source of information. The list of victims in Sarajevo in the period between 1992 and 1994. That list was never completed, and the data from that list was never published. I can demonstrate here today using the authentic statements of Dr. Tabeau, the bureau director, my own affidavit, and the statement taken from Dr. Sestanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Pardon me for interrupting, but there's a distinction here that's being missed. I'm not asking you about the sources that she was relying on. I'm asking you about theoretically whether you believe that this formula is valid mathematically. That's the question. Not about in this case with different sources, just is it a valid formula?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at it as isolated from the phenomenon it's supposed to be applied to, it might be seen as valid. However, the application is wrong because when information was calculated using that formula, non-existent information was used. So what do you end up with? A totally fictitious figure, which means nothing at all. That is the gist about Sarajevo. May I just add one thing. How can it be a census procedure is underway for two years, when according to UN standards applied throughout the world, you must do it in no more than two weeks? The procedure takes no more than two weeks, whereas here you have a census effort that was two years underway, and then you find information suggesting that the project started in 1994, and yet elsewhere the author claims the information is not fit to be published because the software available is insufficient. That is less than serious way --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to treat important information like this, and that is what really chiefly and above all undermines Dr. Tabeau's report. You have it right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Professor, we're done talking about the census.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information does not exist. You won't find it anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Professor, we're done talking about the census. I'm asking you about this theory, and I would challenge that notion that it was done in two years. It was done in 15 days. There's evidence of that in the Tabeau report. I'm not going to ask you about that. I want to get back to this capture-recapture question, because you claim that it's absurd to use a Muslim funeral home as one of the two independent sources to calculate death rates in Sarajevo, but you're -- you're ignoring how she estimated death rates for Muslims first and then she applied the same rate to other ethnicities. That was the methodology she used. So you can't say that other ethnicities are being missed or left out of this approach; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I'll answer by way of metaphor. If you have theory with no practice, it's empty. If you have practice with no theory, it's blind. And that is what you might choose to apply here. So you have a theoretical formula which is then erroneously applied or, rather, the statistics applied in order to test drive the formula is entirely erroneous because it doesn't even exist. The result thereby obtained is devoid of any value at all. Dr. Tabeau had nothing but the best intentions to use this table and then apply this formula to this table containing figures. The information was never published. That is the problem. Could we please scan the information that I'm offering, authentic data that I brought along. This is a very important source and I have it here with me in my set, and that applies to all the players throughout these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I want to ask you just a few questions about your Srebrenica component of your report before we close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, could I -- I wanted to note that doctor's report has two para 9 -- 47s. So I was confused. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 47 appears after 48 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm now looking at page 106 of your report in English at the bottom. At and certain point the paragraph numbers stop so I'm going to use page numbers, and this is page 105 of the B/C/S at the bottom. So now we're talking about the Srebrenica report that Dr. Tabeau issued, and you say in this paragraph: "The standard statistical method of matching is not applied correctly." And then in the next paragraph, this is on English page 107, B/C/S page 105, you say that by applying "a correct methodological approach, it's possible to identify 16 per cent of persons in the 1991 census." Now, I'm sure you will recall having read Dr. Tabeau's report, which P4995, that there is an extensive discussion of academic literature and approaches to data matching in Annex 5. That's pages 67 to 76 of her report. And then in Annex 6 there's a detailed discussion of how the matching approaches were used for each data source, and that's at page 77 to page 104. Now, by contrast you just say standard statistical method of matching is not applied correctly, and then you have this figure, 16 per cent, which it looks to me like you pull out of thin air. So I'm right when I say that there's nowhere in your report where you explain what this correct methodological report is or how you generated a number like 16 per cent; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is a very complex problem and something that we have addressed before. The matching method is a pattern used by Dr. Tabeau. The results thereby obtained -- obtained are in this case not as reliable as she claims. We used our own calculations and we were only able to identify a total of 16 per cent such persons based on what we called the identification key, which is what we demonstrate in table 1, the discrepancies in terms of matching, table 1 and table 2. Persons who actually exist and persons who actually don't exist. And were they taken into account when doing the actual matching procedure or not. So there's your best illustration, and it's no more than a couple of examples really.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the methodology never had any hope of delivering valid data. That is the gist of our complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So that's the only support for this. It's this table 1 and table 2 which show up on page 111 of your report which are literally just lists of four names and showing how there's a difference in the date of birth in four records. There's no calculation, there's no explanation of what kind of identification key you're talking about or how it was applied. That doesn't appear anywhere in this report.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our opinion that would have gone too far, stating all the identification keys. If you want to challenge a theory, you need something representative, a single example such as tables 1 and 2, thereby undermining another expert's decision to use the methods that they did. Why would we go on using 15, 20, 50 different tables if we can only use two and it's all there for all to see? You have information under A here, information under B. It's quite obvious that the names are the same, the father's names are the same, birth years are different, but the identification figures are all the same. So this is very confusing. It creates a muddle in the head of anyone looking into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it was quite sufficient for us to show this in order to demonstrate that the method would not be delivering any valid results.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about page 110 in English in the middle of the page and page 109 in B/C/S at the top half of the page, because here you claim that Dr. Tabeau's report automatically excludes any match of a name on the missing-persons' list and an identical name on the voters register in a different part of the country; right? The part of the quote -- the part that you quote says: "A match of missing people and registered voters was not accepted if the locations were clearly inconsistent; for example, if a person was born, lived, and went missing in Eastern Bosnia according to the missing lists but registered to vote in and for a municipality in a completely different part of the country according to the voter list." And then in the following paragraphs of your report you use this quote essentially to accuse Dr. Tabeau of intentionally dismissing evidence that an alleged Srebrenica victim might be alive and registering to vote somewhere else. Now, have I accurately described your objection?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have accurately described it, but it is not my intention to accuse anyone of anything. We are simply disagreeing about facts, because Dr. Tabeau used a method that in our submission is impractical, inaccurate, and impracticable. So we're trying to build our own case to show why that is so without in any way intending to impeach anyone or indeed accuse anyone of deliberately trying to conceal something, but we don't necessarily agree on the methodology, and you know, we researchers normally say in science there can be no compromise.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Perhaps I used the wrong word. You're not accusing her, but you're saying she's wrong, and I think this is different from what she actually says in her report, at P4995, which I think we should call up now at page 73, because I think it's important to show what she actually wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Is this the right page? There we go. It's the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: What you can see here is she's describing how it was difficult to match the ICRC and PHR missing persons lists with the 1997 voters register because they produced -- those two databases did not have very many variables in common and the result was that they produced lots of extra potential matches that could not be excluded by other variables. So the issue here was to identify matches that might be potentially false and then inspect them more closely. Now, as it's apparent from this middle paragraph, the quote that you pulled related to this process. The idea was that a match could not be automatically accepted if there were location inconsistencies. And in the key part which you don't mention in your report, in the next paragraph, what we see is that data from the 1991 census was used to verify the potential matches because there's more data in census records. They overlapped much more comprehensively with both missing persons lists and the voters register. So you can see that by comparing these records with the census they could see if they were really the same person or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do you have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It's the paragraph that starts with: "The use of data from the 1991 census was crucial in concluding whether a pair of potential matches of records from two different lists represented the same person." It's that paragraph, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So my question for you, Professor, is that using the quotation that you did to assert that Dr. Tabeau was intentionally ignoring evidence that an alleged Srebrenica victim might be alive and registering to vote somewhere else is actually highly misleading based on what she actually wrote in her report. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm unable to accept that. I'm trying to not use these cumbersome words such as "ignoring something" or "someone" and so on and so forth. But that doesn't necessarily mean that I agree with the method she used when comparing all that information. The matching method for us is the method that gets the best results, the most reliable results. That is not necessarily our position but that is the position taken by Dr. Tabeau in her report. We are changing tack here using a different method to so that that is not necessarily the case, and we applied that idea, that method to Srebrenica and all the other information, particularly in view of the fact that the checklist for the 1997, 1998 register is entirely inaccurate. Dr. Tabeau also talks about voluntary voters' registers. What does that mean, voluntary? That means it's not necessarily something you must do. You choose whether you want to go along or not. What does that mean? And I think all of our discrepancies actually stem from that regarding the information presented by Dr. Tabeau. So that is the gist of this schism between the two approaches and then that leads to further discrepancies down the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. File, the quotation that you referred to is one referred to in footnote 57 in Dr. Pasalic's report. Page 110.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then if you are putting that that's a misrepresentation, why don't we take a look at the actual paragraph Doctor refers to?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: We have, Mr. President, and perhaps I wasn't clear enough in explaining, but that comes from the sentence just above the paragraph that I was referring to. It's on the same page that's currently up in e-court. You can see at the bottom of the paragraph essentially in the middle of the page it says: "A match of missing people and registered voters was not accepted," and then it goes on, and that's the sentence the Professor is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the Professor put footnote 57 [Realtime transcript read in error "67"] and refers to pages 6 and pages 16 of two reports. Did you check that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I did. Those are old reports and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that's an erroneous quotation is it your submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It's a -- it's a correct quotation, but the -- the text of the annex is the same. In other words, in -- in all versions of these reports, this description of the process is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Footnote 57 or footnote 67 as the LiveNote states, which is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I said footnote 57.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I wasn't going to address this but because you just mentioned it, this question of the voluntary registration, I just want to -- I just want to point you to a comment that Dr. Tabeau makes in P4993, which is at page 219, where she's describing this voters register, and she says: "The total population of the country was approximately 4.3 million in 1991, whereas an estimate of 3.4 million people was given for 1995 by the 1998 world population prospects, United Nations 1999. It is clear that the 2.13 million voters constitute a large and reliable sample of the 18-plus population. Its size is big enough to prevent errors related to the persons not registering to vote." So my understanding is that you just have a disagreement with Dr. Tabeau about whether this is a representative sample or not. Is that -- that's the nature of your disagreement. And if you could just answer with a yes or a no I'd appreciate it, because we only have one set of questions left.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just very briefly. Where does Dr. Tabeau get the information back 1995 there were 3.4 million inhabitants there overall? No one ever presented that particular calculation. How can you be familiar with certain components of an overall phenomenon if you're wrong about the whole. We don't have the estimate issued by any public institution from 1996, so it's all speculation. That's what I'm trying to say. Now, where did she arrive by matching the 1997, 1998 information 200.000 people, 300.000 people, 3 million people? If she has something official to show for it, perhaps she should come forward and do so. I demonstrated that two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. A different subject. You served for a period of time as deputy minister for education in Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And in 2006, Milorad Dodik proposed to appoint you as the RS minister of education but that was blocked by the Office of the High Representative; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was never shown that. This is a result of some disagreements within the political party to which I then belonged, but there were no formal official challenges by the High Representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there was no reason for anything to be challenged.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the office the High Representative objected to Serb nationalist commentary that was appearing in children's school textbooks that you were authoring?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: National commentary you're talking about is something quite random. The textbooks are written according to established programmes and plans. I happened to be one of the authors. These books are regularly reviewed and very favourably, so all they reflect is something that is part of the curriculum for students of a certain age. Now, whether anyone actually liked these books or not, well, that's another matter all together, but these books have been in use for a full 10 years and they are still being republished. So that tells you all you need to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I understand your point, but I am actually interested in whether other people liked these books, and in particular I'm interested in whether or not the Office of the High Representative had a problem with the content of the books which caused you not to be appointed as RS minister of education. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question. Back in 2001 when I was deputy minister of education, we tried to agree on something called the core curriculum at the republic level back then, and that also included the textbooks that I co-authored. There were different views being expressed, so we used the standardised set of these core criteria, and these have been used for 12 years in Bosnia-Herzegovina, ever since 2001 across Bosnia-Herzegovina because the jurisdiction for education is on Republika Srpska as an entity, the 10 cantons and the Brcko district. It's not down to Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole. My conviction about the -- what was the case back in 1996 has nothing to do with my scientific research and me as the author of those textbooks. It was more of a political conviction on part. It's due to a change in that situation that I quit the party and quit my political position, the office that I held back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we have time, could we just look at 65 ter number 24762, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: What you'll see in the B/C/S version in a lower left is an article in Oslobodjenje from 25 February 2006, and in the first paragraph it says: "The PM designate for the composition of the new Government of Republika Srpska, Milorad Dodik, declared on Friday in Banja Luka that Anton Kasipovic should be appointed to the position of minister of education of Republika Srpska, because during the verification phase the OHR had objections on the proposal to appoint Stevo Pasalic from the party of democratic progress to the function. Pasalic is currently assistant to minister of education of Republika Srpska, and according to Dodik the OHR had certain objections to his work on preparations of school books." Now, did Mr. Dodik ever tell you about those objection?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the best illustration of how journalists take great liberties in erroneously interpreting a subject matter. I wasn't a member of Milorad Dodik's party back then, firstly. Secondly, I was not directly in touch with him. Thirdly, we're not talking about the information presented here. This is all off the record chitchat and rumours. These are not authorised pieces that were eventually published. I deemed this to be entirely unimportant. Why didn't anyone just decide to pick up the phone, call me, and ask me to make a statement? This is entirely irrelevant. This is just politics. It's not scientific research. And politics where I come from is a complex matter. Take my word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And so my final question then is yesterday, when you were talking about being awarded a medal by the President of Republika Srpska for outstanding scientific research, the Njegos medal, is this by any chance the same person - this is Milorad Dodik - who gave you that award; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a medal, it's a decoration, as we say. Njegos, first rank. Milorad Dodik is President of Republika Srpska, it's an institution, and he happens to be the incumbent right now. There's a procedure when these high decorations are rewarded. There's a selection process, and then the final stage where the eventual decision is taken, and this is where the president of the republic gets involved. It's obviously an enormous honour for each citizen to be awarded this highest of all possible state decorations for his professional activity. Needless to say, I am very proud of my achievement and of being awarded this decoration for my scientific research, because that is all I got it for.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 10 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning. To everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to start with the latest topic dealt with. Can you tell us how this -- how these supposed 2.13 million voters, in what relation do they stand to my 20 municipalities and how these 20 municipalities of mine could be representative or perhaps what kind of conclusion can one draw from this?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat what we have been saying already. Twenty municipalities and such examples are not a representative sample by a long shot, the more so since these municipalities were selected on a less than neutral basis, and they do not reflect the entire process that's being dealt with in the Tabeau report. Therefore, the results arrived at by the OTP experts are irrelevant, because they have no practical significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 20 of today's transcript, you were asked why -- or how come you observed the fact -- the unusual fact that Croatia is publishing demographic data of a neighbouring country. So let me ask you if Croatia took part militarily in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially, I'm not a military expert, but it's a notorious fact that Croatia did take part, active part, in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we can establish a link between that and the fact that a statistical bulletin was printed there that included the census results. This is inappropriate, but the facts are beyond dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Has Bosnia ever been part of a Croatian state?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Whoever knows how the Kingdom of Serbs, Croatians, and Slovenians came about in 1918, which then became the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in 1929, knows that there were banovinas or perhaps counties in that country. One of them was the Croatian Banovina, and this is sometimes mentioned even today in historical context to illustrate the pretensions or Croatia's aspirations to parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Croatia initiate trials that included demographic issues?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There have been such initiatives. I observed them in the 20 years I followed this subject matter. From professional circles or institutional circles we can say that these initiatives are unfounded or blown out of proportion from the aspect of demography and some other aspects. Some expert reports that had such aspirations in the area of demography have been rejected before this court, and they were drafted by some Croatian experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 7 of today's transcript, you were asked about the error of a one-sided approach to a complex phenomenon, and you answered that question or those questions. The inclusion of the -- of another aspect such as the demographic movements of Serbian population, how does that affect the relative ratios of other populations and demographic movements?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, it absolutely affects them. A relative number stands for a relative share in something, but when you also have another component, namely an absolute number, which includes that process, then the relative indicators change. One -- one relative number can rise, whereas another can diminish. And it is very important to include the Serbian population and other populations in order to get an overall picture of a complex process. A partial observation of a process will not give a relevant result. In fact, it will depict a distorted historical image without any value.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us very briefly for what reasons or, rather, what can cause the diminution of the share of one population in the overall population? For example, the share of Muslims in one municipality. How can it be changed and on what does it depend?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several factors that can affect that share, and that's why a partial approach is not valid. For example, there can be temporary movements out of one territory due to combat activities. That territory may be controlled by the army of that ethnic group, or there can be movements out of towns to rural areas, and there can either be motives such as economic or joining families. There are a number of factors that can bring about such changes, and these changes in the movement of persons were not taken into consideration in the OTP report. This is what we call the principle of connected vessels in demography. It is present in all demographic movements in BH, especially during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you about one municipality. Bosanska Krupa is excluded. Now, how would you characterise the displacement of population from Bosanska Krupa which was a combat area to Sanski Most in the same entity of the RS? Would you characterise that as a persecution and ethnic cleansing or differently?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already answered that question. This is conscious movement of population to a safer place to protect them from combat activity. So not the expulsion of non-Serb population by Serbian military formations but, rather, providing safety to the population at another place because they would be jeopardised by combat activities. This can by no means be characterised as ethnic cleansing, because it is differently motivated. Ethnic cleansing is a fast and forcible removal of population from a certain territory. That is the international definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How does the right to return -- in what connection is the right of return with ethnic cleansing? Does the right to return affect that notion at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure this is a field to be covered by the Doctor's expertise. In the cross-examination, the issue of ethnic cleansing was not dealt with in that sense. I would like you to move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 6 of today's transcript you mentioned that sometimes it is possible to research and -- the whole population, and in some cases you must work with samples. What should be given a priority? What is more accurate even under the conditions that would allow an ideally representative sample?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No matter what the sample is like, even the most representative one cannot give such precise data that the entire population can give. So priority is certainly to be given to the whole population, because that will yield an absolutely accurate result.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us in what condition Yugoslavia was and the notion of being Yugoslav in 1991 with regard to the political processes in Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The topic of being Yugoslav. I ask to be allowed to introduce the question to provide a basis. I will not ask leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That was my objection -- my objection was not about the subject, it was about the form of the question and the content which is vague. I don't think that's going to produce a helpful answer, in what condition Yugoslavia was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see how Mr. Karadzic is going to reformulate his question. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Professor Pasalic, in 1991, declaring oneself as Yugoslav, did it mean the same thing as before 1990 when the first multi-party elections were held, or did it change due to some political processes in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1991 census in all of Yugoslavia took place under conditions of strong political and ethnic tensions. There were clear ambitions for the succession of Slovenia, Croatia, and other Yugoslav republics, and the census showed that in those republics that artificial category of Yugoslavs had practically disappeared from their census results. It still existed in Serbia among the Serbian population that was traditionally connected with that category of being Yugoslav. We have shown that in all censuses preceding 1991. That is why we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the expert please repeat the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you start over again after you referred to census -- "in all censuses preceding 1991."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If I understand correctly, the 1991 census was taken in all of Yugoslavia except Kosovo and Metohija. It was clear at that time that the census was burdened by political and ethnic tensions, that there were clear ambitions by some of the then Yugoslav republics, Slovenia, Croatia, and others, to secede from Yugoslavia, and in the censuses in that -- those republics, the number of Yugoslavs suddenly dropped, whereas that category had been significantly present in earlier censuses. A higher number of Yugoslavs was present in Serbia and in areas where the Serbs were the majority population. That is why we -- we criticise the -- we object to the category of Yugoslavs in Bosnia-Herzegovina and subsuming it under "others," because in the 1991 census there were many dozen ethnicities under "others." The 1991 census held in Yugoslavia differed in that respect from all other -- other previous censuses, and there had been a number of censuses. The first one was held in 1948, and it went on until 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]
