utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 82 of today's transcript, you were asked -- or, rather, on page 82 of your report, you were asked why you object to the validity of the voters register in 1997. Now, supposing that the same kind of source had been used in 1997, namely a census, would the inclusion of one pre-war year and two post-war years would have affected -- would it affect the research into the demographic consequences of the war, that is one pre-war year and two post-war years? Even under ideal conditions.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even under ideal conditions, the 1991 census and a supposed 1997 or 1998 census would not have produced identical results even without the war. Since there was a war, some processes were generated or, rather, intensified, but from the professional point of view, it is unacceptable to compare the results of the 1991 census, which was held under peacetime conditions, with the 1997 results which were never verified as a primary source. That's what I meant when I was speaking about comparing apples and pears, because those -- those data were not collected with the same methods, because one of them was taken based on a sample and on a voluntary inclusion in the voters register, and then from that you infer conclusions. We missed 22 years of primary data sources from 1991 on. Without them we cannot draw valid conclusions. Today, this is the greatest burden for all strategic planning in Bosnia-Herzegovina, without even going into the post-war period. But let me conclude. Demographic movements, globally speaking, and this includes Bosnia-Herzegovina, have been very intensive. That is why I wanted to stress in this report that demographic losses must be viewed from all aspects for the period of the past 20 years, and that can produce valid results.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have occasion to observe whether demographic movements and changes existed in 1991 up until April 1992 when the war broke out and whether they were excluded or at least underlined in the findings of the OTP experts? How can they be separated from the wartime developments?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. There were such demographic movements before the war when the populations migrated within Bosnia-Herzegovina and outside Bosnia-Herzegovina because they were beginning to feel insecure and feared the possible breaking out of a war because there were ethnic tensions that were rising up until the event of the war, and then there are the changes and demographic movements after the war. So if we look at them in the first, second, and third stage, only by doing that can we actually draw accurate conclusions about the movements in general. Now, in those pre-war -- in the pre-war period, if I am correct, if I recall this correctly, they were -- that was completely ignored in the OTP expert's reports, but they were very important. It would be very interesting to analyse why those changes began in late 1991 and then 1992, and then the intensity changes during the war period of those movements, and then there is another period, the third stage after the war when the intensity changed again. So these three periods are very significant for any kind of serious research.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where can we find the results of these movements of demographic changes before the war, during it, and afterwards?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I object at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm going to object at this point. I didn't ask him about the parts of his report relating to the demographic changes before and after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the Prosecutor challenged the position of Professor Pasalic, claiming that the census -- his position on the unreliability of the register's votes of 1997. So what I'm trying to ask here is this: Even had this census had been ideal --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There is a lot of noise. We could not hear the last portion of the -- of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You were not heard. The last part of your comments were not heard. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said, but I'm not sure what has been recorded in the transcript. The OTP raised this issue. They challenged the validity of comparing two sources, two types of data sources, that Professor Pasalic did between 1991 and 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So my question is this: Even if this had been a census and not voters' registers, how would that have affected the outcome and where can we see that -- what would the consequences have been had the two post-war years and the last year of the war been included, because two of those years were non-war years, but they have been represented as years that were the consequence of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, absolutely. We wanted to show that after the post-war period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pause. Pause, please. Yes, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: My observation is that the 1997 census as a source is perfectly acceptable as a subject for questioning. That does not offer any insight into what happened before the war, which is part of the question that Dr. Karadzic asked about, and I didn't ask any questions about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we have to see whether it has any relation or bearing on the accuracy of the census if it had taken place. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will allow the question. Yes, Dr. Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Observing the phenomena right before the war from the census in 1991 and then demographic changes in the course of the war and the demographic changes of the three post-war years, this is extremely important in any research. According to our opinion and our research, the OTP expert reports have simplified this process to a large degree, and they only matched information and data between 1991 and 1997 as their -- as if there had been nothing happening in those other years in between. So that is why we challenged the voluntary voters register as invalid. That cannot be used as a primary data source because it is irrelevant for what had happened in the war period, because this was happening three years after the war where a lot of people were already migrating out of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, on the other hand, there was a number of people returning to Bosnia and Herzegovina. As I explained yesterday, about 500.000 people returned to Bosnia and Herzegovina, 527.000 remained abroad wanting to become permanent residents there, but there was another process at the same time in those post-war years, people leaving Bosnia-Herzegovina. So we can prove this. There are only four regions in BH today that have a larger number of residents than they had before the war. That's Tuzla, Sarajevo, Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the other areas have lower numbers of residents than in 1991. So this is what we mean when we call -- when we talk about aggregate demographic losses in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but this is something that the Prosecutor did not go into at all, or, rather, its experts. They simplified these demographic changes and movements which then produces a distorted statistic and a distorted picture of all of those events, and this is what we've been persistently trying to show, that you have to shed some light on all of these three stages and their causality, the stage between the war, during the war, and after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the war. [B/C/S spoken] [No interpretation] [In English] Before the war, during the war, and after the war. [Interpretation] Thank you. I will be done very soon, but could you please tell us before that what happened with the activities of the High Representative -- or, rather, were you disqualified by a decision taken by the High Representative?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I insisted on getting some kind of written record of this, but I never received anything either oral -- orally or in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But were some people excluded from all political -- disqualified from all political rights and even some normal work rights, and how widespread was this?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is well known that that was the case. I don't know exactly the number. A large number of people were disqualified, but as we know, many of them in the meantime have returned and were re-included in all the processes. They returned to their work in the political arena, but I was never on any such list, nor was I ever prohibited from doing any kind of work in this entire 20-year period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that some of those people were disqualified and suspicious, deemed suspicious because they assisted me --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is starting to become an argumentative question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And has nothing to do with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it does have to do with the cross-examination. The question is the significance that should be placed on the decisions -- or, rather, not decisions but indications that there were decisions taken by the High Representative, and this was something raised by the Prosecution. The Prosecution introduced this topic of the High Representative, and I just wanted to see what weight can be given to his actions let alone to his presumed intentions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with alleged assistance to you. Shall we move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, excuse me, Mr. President. I think Dr. Karadzic's point here is that the Office of High Representative disqualified a number of people because they had assisted Dr. Karadzic when in fact they hadn't, and therefore accusations made by that same office about the -- Dr. Pasalic are entitled to less weight than they might otherwise appear to be from the Prosecution's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But he should have put that in a neutral way instead of leading -- in such a leading way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if he could reformulate the question but ask on that same topic, I think that would be a good solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I don't think this witness is here to talk about the decisions of the High Representative with regard to other individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you raised the issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I did, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- to challenge the credibility of the witness or for whatever purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think this point is a point for argument. It's not for this witness to give evidence about unless there's some kind of foundation for his knowledge of the actions of the High Representative, but that hasn't been established yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let's see whether Mr. Karadzic has some foundational question. Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, but I have a problem with my old habits when I was from the prosecutorial period where I put leading questions, but I'll try to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know -- were you aware of what -- what attitude the High Representative and what treatment he meted out against individuals that he felt or considered had some kinds of -- some kind of thing with me?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am a public figure, and I'm very well aware of all the developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that's also necessary for my professional work, and I absolutely know, and I know the names of the persons who were disqualified by the High Representative, and that was a large number, claiming that they directly assisted in or participated in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what, if anything, out of all that turned out to be correct? Was it ever established in a relevant -- in a relevant way that someone was disqualified just -- that it was justified in some cases?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, practically all of these individuals were -- it was -- they were relieved of all these charges and no one has ever proved that any of these individuals ever participated in any of the actions that were -- that they were suspected of. So what everybody knows, that is what I know, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor Pasalic. I have no further questions. Thank you for coming to testify, although you have a cold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Professor Pasalic. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for hearing me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the next witness, the Chamber now turns to the accused's notice of a special defence of reprisals as to count 11 filed on the 14th of December, 2012. Having reviewed this notice and the Prosecution's submission filed on the 5th of March, 2013, the Chamber finds that reprisals does not constitute a "special defence" under Rule 67(B) of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. It is a general defence that is best addressed in the judgement if raised and necessary following the conclusion of the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I hope Mr. Robinson understood it better than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understood it, Mr. President, and I'll discuss it with Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We need to observe a pause between questions and answers and also speak slowly so that everything can be recorded. As for the pause to be observed, you can follow the interpretation on the screen. When it stops, we can go on. Did you give a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were in haste to answer my question. Please observe a pause.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D7196. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the statement that we have just addressed, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please don't be confused by the redactions. The Chamber has its reasons, thinking that some of the elements contained in your statement might unnecessarily encumber these proceedings. Did you read and sign this statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown the last page for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this statement a faithful reflection of what you told the Defence team that interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were I to ask you these same questions today, would your answers in essence still be the same?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, in essence they would.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this statement under 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No objection. I was just a little bit concerned about the answer to the question: "Q. Is this statement a faithful reflection of what you told the Defence team that interviewed you? "A. I think so, yes." I don't know if that has some doubt built into it of whether it is a faithful reflection or "accurate" to use the wording from the Statute of what he said. I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you signed this statement did you read it before you signed it? Did you notice anything that needed changing or anything that was inaccurate or inaccurately reflected?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I read the statement. I don't think any changes have to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3126, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to read out a summary of Mr. Nikolic's statement, after which I would like to show him a document. I would like to appeal to the other party's understanding, because we failed to notify them in good time, although the document has been around for a very long time. It is 1D7910. So perhaps they would like to have a look while I read the summary. The relevant page -- pages are 18 and 19. These are the two pages that I will be showing the witness. I will read the summary in English. [In English] Jovan Nikolic was born on 25th of October, 1948, in the village of Kravica, Bratunac municipality. He currently resides there and is the principal of the Branko Radicevic primary school in Bratunac. Following the killings of a Serb and Muslim in August 1970, Muslim-Serb relations in Bratunac municipality worsened. Serious incidents during 1990-1991 caused tensions to escalate. For instance, the SDA Muslim party refused to obey the JNA and instead created their own Territorial Defence. Other incidents included an altercation in Bratunac over the removal of conscript records and the establishment of nightly village guard duties in response to provocation by the Muslim population in the Kravica settlement. As a member of the Municipal Board of the SDS, Jovan Nikolic attended board sessions that assessed the existing political situation and discussed means of peaceful settlement. The SDA Muslim party members frequently attended these meetings. All completed agreements to divide the municipality and the police forces had been annulled due to the complication and further disagreement by Miroslav Deronjic and Ljubo Simic. In April 1992, a Crisis Staff was established composing of individuals holding key positions in the municipality, including Jovan Nikolic himself. The Crisis Staff initiated a decision to disarm all individuals who owned weapons illegally. After an unsuccessful attempt, a second attempt was scheduled to take place on the 9th of May, 1992, to disarm extremists in the Glogova village. However, in Srebrenica on the 8th of May, 1992, the Muslims killed Goran Zekic, a national deputy and president of the Municipal Board of the SDS in Srebrenica and a respected judge. This event, along with the previous deaths of Serb volunteer -- Serbs volunteering to leave their municipality caused the situation to get out of control. Jovan Nikolic states that the killing of Muslims in the Glogova area was not intended by anyone in the municipal or military leadership, nor had a decision to that effect been adopted. Muslim paramilitary units attacked Kravica for the first time on the 27th of May, 1992. From then on, attacks occurred almost every day, including a large-scale attack on the 7th of January. This is 1993. This is Orthodox Christian Christmas. This attack in Kravica resulted in 46 deaths, 86 wounded, and approximately 750 houses burnt down. On the 24th of December, 1992, Mr. Jovan Nikolic was wounded during an attack and been declared permanent disability. Due to his disability, Jovan Nikolic was no longer militarily engaged and instead was appointed as a director of agricultural co-operative in Bratunac in February 1995. After significant riots at the Kravica co-operative sector on the 14th of July, 1995, Jovan Nikolic went to the Bratunac municipality to inform authorities of the incident. Upon being informed, the municipal authorities immediately took action to clean up the terrain with bodies of those killed being transported and buried in Glogova. As a member of the Kravica Territorial Defence Staff and the municipal board of SDS, Jovan Nikolic participated in discussions to allow a humanitarian convoy for Srebrenica to pass through. It was President Radovan Karadzic who had encouraged the population of Kravica to allow this convoy to pass through. Jovan Nikolic never witnessed President Radovan Karadzic issuing any orders that endangered the safety of Muslims in Bratunac and contends that President Radovan Karadzic was not aware of the incidents that had occurred in Bratunac at that time. [Interpretation] And now could we please have 1D7910. It used to be 65 ter 594, and it might be 52957. Only two pages have been admitted so far at the OTP's request. We want to show the witness something that the OTP failed to show him. The document runs into a total of 22 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we have only English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, that is apparently the case. I will read it, and then Mr. Nikolic can listen to the interpretation. Could we please have page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I will read a portion of the document to you irrespective of your knowledge of English. It will be interpreted to you. These are minutes of a meeting of the Main Board held in Kravica on the 22nd of January, 1992, at 1700 hours. First of all, could you please tell us what the phrase means, the Main Board. Is that the municipal Main Board?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the municipal board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have the agenda there, police situation in Yugoslavia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina and how it affects life in the municipality. Is that, sir, what you had in mind in your statement when you said that political issues were considered?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Municipal Board of the SDS very often reviewed the political situation, the security-related situation across the municipality. Based on that, they adopted a number of conclusions with a view to stabilising the situation throughout the municipal territory and also keeping in mind the talks that were underway at the time with SDA representatives in Bratunac. The Municipal Board of the SDS initially entertained very good relations with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll read back to you what Mr. Deronjic, who is the president of the Municipal Board, said by way of introduction. I'll read this in English and you will be receiving interpretation. "[In English] Serbian politics led and represented by Milosevic in Serbia, Karadzic in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Babic in Krajina in sustaining a defeat after defeat. National goals of the Serbian population are not known. The basic programme of the SDS were preservation of Yugoslavia with its all six republics." [Interpretation] And so forth. Do you remember and is this something that was normally the case for the work of the president and other authorities to be considered and analysed at board meetings such as this one?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That was not the established practice, but the meeting in question here did have that kind of character. There was a concern, understandably bearing in mind our situation in the territory at the time, about these things. I would not like to go into what Deronjic said or may have meant, but the prevailing view was that given the situation, the relationship, the good relations between the various ethnic groups in Bratunac would be lost despite which a common state should survive and make it through these difficult times. There was to be no particular anxiety about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why am I criticised here by the late Mr. Deronjic? Is it for extremism or is it for moderation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic -- Mr. Nicholls. My apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honours. I didn't before, but first he read part of the statement -- oh, sorry, the document to the witness and then asked is this what was considered at these meetings, rather than asking what types of things regarding the leadership were discussed at these meetings and then possibly showing him the statement and asking how does this fit in. So it was very leading. He's now asking him to read the statement -- the document, rather, and say what it says about Mr. Deronjic. He should just -- assuming the witness could even know what was in Mr. Deronjic's mind when he's making these criticisms, he should just ask a question before using this statement because it's direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That must be very helpful to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The meeting was initiated precisely for the reasons that I stated before. The people were showing up here were people in key positions for the Serbs. As I said a while ago, the focus was on more tolerance and flexibility about issues that were crucial to the Serbs across the Podrinje region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Simic [Realtime transcript read in error "Simatovic"] is here quoted as saying that he supports Mr. Deronjic's position, and in the last two lines say: "[In English] If it is necessary, we would call off the obedience to Sarajevo, but we should not abandon or let down the people in Bratunac who trust us and in whom we trust." [Interpretation] Could I have the next page now, please. Here's your reply, page --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm trying to keep up with this -- with no notice of the document. What Mr. Karadzic read out is not exactly what Ljubisav Simic said. It says "Simatovic" in the transcript. Mr. Karadzic said "call off the obedience to Sarajevo," whereas it says: "We have many other things in Bratunac to deal -- to be dealt with --" sorry: "If it is necessary, we would call off the obedience to Sarajevo." So that may make a difference to the witness rather than posing it as a decision which has been made or is a recommendation that's unconditional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he read that part but because of overlapping it was not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In that case I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your intervention. But shall we continue. When you switch from B/C/S to English, you should put a pause.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will now show you what you said back then. It is at the bottom of page 19. This is not the right page. Or maybe the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Nineteen, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Mr. Jovan Nikolic: I suggest that during the meeting with him we inform Karadzic that conveying the information from the top to the bases is a problem. Second issue is regarding the option to have Kulin as a currency. The third issue is related to a referendum." [Interpretation] Can you tell us what you meant when you said that there were problems in January before the war with passing down information top down?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It follows from the discussion at this meeting that we didn't have enough information. That is why we see here -- we see it stated that all information that is significant come from the right source. Your name is mentioned here among others. There were many problems. We were puzzled because we didn't have enough information. We erred. That is why I said that we need information from the right source so that we're sure what -- what things are like. There were different interpretations by Deronjic and other people who were in the highest echelons of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did this information interpreted in such a way reach you, and did it prove accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The president of the Municipal Board of our party, Mr. Deronjic, was a hard-working man, but he also had some character traits which were not impeccable. He was a leader, but he wanted to be even more of a leader. Whenever he wasn't able to impose his will, he would refer to President Karadzic and other men or persons of authority and subsequently would learn that that was unfounded. So there was the opinion in the board that it would be best that information we needed to know be presented through documents and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did -- how was information flow during the war as compared to the pre-war period?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, the effects of the war could be felt. A number of members joined the military units. I was one. I went to the Kravica local commune where I was born and we dealt with the war. We had huge problems defending the village. Some people went over to the other side and communication was very difficult. It was very hard to bring together the Municipal Board, but still some people were able to meet and discuss things from the aspect of politics and based on the information that had arrived. I was not very actively involved in political life after April because we had a lot to do at Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's please go to page 21. The transcript does not reflect that Kravica was left without communication lines and that's why there was no political life.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Adequate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Maybe I should read this out to you in English: "Mr. Jovan Nikolic said that he spoke with the people and that the Crisis Staff would be established within few days and would be functional. From the item 1 of the agenda, we moved on to the item 2. Miroslav said that the contacts with the army are established and that few companies should be formed which would be subordinated to and --" [Interpretation] And then it was not recorded. What was envisaged? Who should your TO companies be subordinate to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The circumstances in our municipality, the precarious situation, including the political situation, resulted in the establishment of some bodies, and by agreement and also based on need, a crisis staff for Bratunac municipality was formed. The military authorities, that is, the army, who were partly present in town and the TO should deal with military matters, whereas Crisis Staffs should deal with creating conditions, monitoring the political situation, and some sort of co-ordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's have the next page, please. Just the first line. Can you tell us if you had any talks with the military. It says here: "[In English] Jovan Nikolic explained that the talk they had with the army representatives."

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The military was part of the operative structures present there, and the army was a sort of guarantee of safety in the territory where we were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellencies, I seek to tender pages 18, 19, 21, and 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't object, Your Honours. I just -- if I caught the date that the statement was signed by the witness, his 92 ter statement, it was the 10th of March. This is the 14th of March. The last time I raised this type of issue with Mr. Robinson, he agreed that it would be better if we got proofing notes with the new information. So I don't object, but I don't know why I didn't get a proofing note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, Mr. President, I wasn't present at this proofing, so I don't know if this subject was discussed with the witness, but Dr. Karadzic can advise the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I thought the -- I thought the whole document had been admitted as P2597, and later it turned out that only individual pages had been admitted. That's the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a separate matter whether you need to inform the other party, the Prosecution, by way of proofing note if something new arises during your proofing. That's the point, isn't it, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. That was a hugely -- a hugely evasive answer by Mr. Karadzic. I think he understands the point is not the fact that he's using this document but that he is asking the witness questions about these meetings, the relationship between the leadership in Bratunac and Mr. Karadzic, and discussions about co-ordinating with the military.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I can clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, did we show you this document during the proofing?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you saw me, did we show you this document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This document? No, not this one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellencies. None of this was part of the proofing. That's why I apologised for not announcing it. We did not use this document during the proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I won't belabour the point, but even if they didn't use the document during the proofing, if they're going to elicit new information from the witness, again I'm not objecting to the document, but we -- we should be given some notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Robinson will have a word with Mr. Karadzic in this regard. I took a look at the exhibit in Karadzic referred to, P2597, but there we have handwritten note in B/C/S original, but we missed the original here. Shall we admit it in full or mark it for identification? Being -- noting that it is unrevised translation, we better mark it for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Reid tells me parts of this are admitted as different exhibits. I'm sure there must be -- that we must be able to connect it up. I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So until then we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We mark it for identification. Page 18 to 21 [sic]. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D3127, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, or you're done?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellencies, and I note the time too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I, Excellency, just one question before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: A question to the witness, okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, there is one thing that I remain unclear about and that I'd like you to clarify. What was the purpose of invoking me whenever something needed doing although you had nothing directly to do with me but, rather, it was always a go-between who invoked my name. Was that for purely political effect or what?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were situations like that, political situations. When I talked about our president Deronjic and the way he established authority. When a decision needed implementing his way, he would simply invoke President Karadzic. Whenever he said, "President Karadzic said this or said that," we would simply accept it. At a later date we go back to it and what we find is that he used your name as an instance of authority in order to implement his own ideas and decisions, personnel-related decisions, appointments, political decisions sometimes. Very often during our Municipal Board meetings, we had no choice but to accept his words at face value because he invoked your name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Nikolic. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As regards the exhibit we marked for identification, I was advised to correct the record as regards the page numbers. We admitted from page 18 to the end, i.e., page 22. Yes, Mr. Nikolic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony in most part, and now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I want to do first is talk about the 14th of July and the critical part of your statement where you describe going to the Kravica warehouse that morning and seeing those terrible sights. Okay?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, let me ask --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just trying to let you know where I'm going. I'll ask some questions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This for Your Honours and everybody is set out at paras 55 and 56 of your statement. I'll just summarise quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Paragraph 55 you came back from Potocari on the 13th where you'd been for just a short time, worked in your office, and then the co-op in Bratunac, went home, and then you talk about how the following day, the 14th, you went -- you say: "I went to my office in the morning where I finished up some work." That's in Bratunac. "After this, I went to Kravica with Dragan Nikolic to see how the purchase of raspberries was unfolding." Then in paragraph 56 you state that you arrived, you stepped out of the car, you saw something strange was happening in front of the warehouse, you saw some people there you didn't recognise. These persons were doing the killing, wearing soldier uniforms, but you could not see any insignia, and they wore some sort of masks over their heads. You couldn't recognise any of these soldiers doing the killing; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. But you could tell that none of them were from Bratunac. That's what it says in your statement that you said didn't need any changes.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you testified here before to basically the same events in the Blagojevic case as a Defence witness; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And there again speaking of the 13th, after you were at your office in Bratunac -- the co-operative in Bratunac, excuse me. After being in Potocari you went home. And then the following day, the 14th, you said: "I went to Kravica around 9.30 or 10.00..."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I should say this is 65 ter 24749 at e-court page 18 and it's T8011.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So you went to Kravica around 9.30 or maybe 10.00 on the morning of the 14th you testified to, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the reason there you said was we had not received any weigh bills, the receipts from the sales point in Kravica, nor had we received a report from the people in charge of selling the raspberries, and so you went there with Dragan Nikolic; right? That's what you testified to.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And then same thing. You see this terrible scene of ten Muslims being laid out flat on the ground and murdered; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, the people you said in soldier uniforms were wearing masks as they committed this crime?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And one thing, sorry, I forgot you were interviewed by the OTP, the Office of the Prosecutor, I mean, in 2001 by Mr. Peter McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that's 65 ter 24751. I'm referring to e-court page 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And there again you said -- what I forgot to ask you is on the 13th of July there you said that you were at home in Bratunac around 10.00 and you didn't see any buses with Muslim prisoners in Bratunac at night on the 13th of July; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And one thing else you were asked about in your interview -- well, I'll strike that. Strike that. Other than this: At e-court page 31 of that interview, and I'm not asking you this as a legal characterisation, but what you saw at the warehouse was so disturbing that you said: "I saw that genocide had been committed in the warehouse. That there was killing, had been killing." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This was 2001. I was a suspect at the time. I was at the military base in Banja Luka. The interview that was conducted did not essentially change later on. Everything that I did on the 13th and the 14th will be reflected equally in all of my later statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there. All I'm asking you is -- I'm only asking you one question which is a yes or no. Do you remember that you described that scene you saw in your words - I'm not saying you're a lawyer - as genocide, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't remember using the word "genocide." If indeed I did use the word then perhaps I wasn't sufficiently and properly informed about the real meaning of the word, and it wasn't my job to know. It certainly was very sad scene, a sad sight. I did what I did for a number of reasons in terms of telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you right --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there because you've answered my question and you're going further. You don't remember if you used the word "genocide."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Could I have 65 ter 24752 up, please. I'll wait for page 1 of the Serbian. All right. Looks like -- maybe Mr. Reid can assist. It looks like page 1 of the Serbian is missing. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. This is 10th October 2005. Bosnia and Herzegovina prosecutor's office. Record of examination of the witness. Present Ibro Bulic, the state court prosecutor; witness, you, Jovan Nikolic; and your lawyer, starting at 13.50. And we can see at the bottom of that first page on the left your signature saying you understand the warning given to you that you have to tell the truth in this statement and that giving a false testimony is a criminal offence; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the last page. Here we are see your signature and the penultimate paragraph in the English and it's the same on your page at the top. "Now, the witness was thereafter advised of his right to have the record read to him before the said record is signed and he says: 'The record has been -- has been read over to me out loud, and I was simultaneously following the text on the monitor, and I do not have any objections to it so I will sign it." And your signature -- this is the question: Your signature is there as well, under witness -- over witness; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, let's go to page 2 of the English, please, and also of the Serbian. Page 3 of the English. Sorry. Sorry, page 4 of the English. I'm sorry. And Serbian page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to go through this signed under penalty statement of yours in some detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page of the Serbian, I think. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, here you begin -- I'm sorry. Page 2 of the Serbian. My mistake. At the bottom. There's a warehouse next to -- this is concerning the 13th of July, 1995, we can see, the 13th of July. And you discuss the Kravica warehouse. Now we can go to the next page of the Serbian, stay where we are in the English. And there you talk about three Kravica farming co-operative workers, Zoran Eric, Milos Djukanovic, and Miladin Nikolic, and they were workers at the warehouse; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were workers at the co-op, employees of the co-op.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And at the time, they happened to be performing this work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Now let's go down. Right where we are in the English is fine. I'm at the lower part of the page. "On 13 July 1995, I was at work. During the day I was in the office in Bratunac as well as the agricultural facilities of the co-operative in Bratunac which are located close to Bratunac." Then we go down a bit. "When -- while I was at the agricultural facilities of the co-operative in Bratunac at around 2200 hundred hours in the evening we decided to go to the Kravica farming co-operative. They were Miladin Jovanovic, Perica Vasovic and Miso Eric there. Together we all set out in the car owned by Miladin Jovanovic." And it says he was driving the car and you arrived at the farming co-operative, that is the warehouse, in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Next page the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "It was dark." So this is night-time. "But it was not very late. It was the summertime and there was no light." Then you talk about how Zoran Eric the employee appeared with the gun, told you to turn off the lights. And before my friend objects, and I am going to ask a question, but this is important background. "When he saw me, Zoran Eric approached telling me that people had been killed there and there were a lot of dead people and that they were Muslims from the area of Srebrenica. He also said that the Special Police from Skelani was there. They had problems regarding the prisoners since not all of them were placed indoors. Zoran Eric also told me that before we arrived, the policeman named Krsto Dragicevic from Skelani had been killed after which the shooting of the prisoners started. At that time a policeman came in front of me." He was dressed in the police fatigues armed with a gun and tried to order you to stand guard. You refused and you didn't have to because you were appointed the manager. You were the manager. "At that time, I heard the burst of fire in the direction of the central part of the hangar and the detonation of bombs were also heard." Then you're asked a question by prosecutor Ibro Bulic about whether you saw other policemen present, and you said you didn't see anybody, but: "By the bursts of fire from several rifles, he concluded that there were more persons who were shooting in the direction of the central entrance to the hangar." So you were at the Kravica warehouse at night on the 13th of July as it says in your sworn statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you were told then that prisoners had been killed in the warehouse; correct? Again as said in your sworn statement.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I said that on the 13th of July at Kravica there had been a serious incident during which the prisoners seized the guards' weapons and opened fire at the guards upon which the guards fired back and killed the men in the hangar. That occurred on the 13th. I happened to be there that evening. I stayed for about five or six minutes after which I drove back to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop, because you've answered the question. I didn't ask you where you went next or how long you stayed. You answered question. You were told that men were murdered there that night. I'll continue on the same page. "On the Prosecutor's question to the witness whether he had found out in any other way as to who could have been the perpetrator of those killings apart from what Zoran Eric told him, that they had been committed by the Special Police from Skelani, the witness states that: "'Already the next day it was a generally known fact and a 'open secret' that they had been committed precisely by the Special Police Unit from Skelani since it was rumoured all around that they had done that and nobody else was mentioned, neither an individual or a unit that could have committed those killings.'" So not only were you told there were killings that night that it was done by the Special Police, but also the next day you were told by farm co-operative workers who were there that it was the Special Police from Skelani. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were not told --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That was -- that was in the evening hours of that day around 5.30 or 6.00, after the incident. There was shooting and in that shooting the commander of the police got killed, and of course we heard which formation that man was belonging to. It was a public secret that the Special Police from Skelani had done that because they -- it was said that they were -- had been doing that on that day. But when I was there in the evening, there were no longer those police officers but other persons, and that's the difference between what you're insisting on and the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what I'm insisting on is that you say in your statement that was sworn and that we will see appears in a judgement of the state court from your testimony there that you saw a policeman there in police fatigues the night of the 13th of July; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: One police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You answered. That was the question. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not the entire answer was recorded. One police officer who appeared before me. This "who appeared before me" part was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, not one word of what we've gone through about your trip to the Kravica warehouse on the 13th of July, 1995, is in your statement which you provided which is now evidence before Their Honours, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, 13th of July, 1995, at night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the 13th of July. That's the date we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And you have not answered my question. You have excised completely from your testimony here the fact that you were present at the Kravica warehouse on July 13th at around 10.00 p.m.; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That was not consciously omitted. I wasn't asked about the 13th, only about the 14th, and I mentioned the 13th of July in all my statements and all evidence. There is no reason for me to conceal anything about the 13th of July. That's the day I came there, when I saw things, and why -- and I returned. The -- including the night of the 13th. In the proofing the 14th was mentioned, and I was focussing on the 14th. However, I'm not evading anything, and I'm ready to tell the Trial Chamber everything I saw there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- you said, Mr. Nikolic, during the proofing the 14th was mentioned and you were focusing on the 14th. What do you mean by that? In what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that in these proofing materials I didn't find the 13th anywhere. I was only asked about the 14th, and that's why my statement mentions the 14th. However, the reason for the omission of the 13th can only be a hazard. It can only be by chance. There's no reason for me to conceal anything I saw on the 13th at Kravica. The day I decided to speak out about the suffering of the Muslims at Kravica, I -- it was clear to me that I wanted for the Serbs to also see the other side. When I came to Kravica to the buildings belonging to the co-op of which I was a director, I saw a horrible sight. A police officer appeared before me, I returned home, and on the 14th my new activities began about the -- by clarifying what had happened on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had huge problems because of my honesty and I was even placed in detention. I was also a witness of the Prosecution and then I was also a witness of the Defence, so I found myself in a precarious situation in that period, the 13th and the 14th. This is probably the worst experience I've had in my life. Later on my brother got killed in the activities around Srebrenica, the fighting. When the Trial Chamber -- and I hope the Trial Chamber understands what I was exposing myself to by testifying about these events rather than putting any kind of or other -- having suspicion against me why I -- why I went to those buildings that belonged to my co-op.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well back to you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you went back to Kravica warehouse again on the 14th of July in the morning, and this is in your statement at paragraph 55 which I read a bit of before. "The following day, 14 July, 1995, I went to my office in the morning where I finished up some work. After this, I went to Kravica with Dragan Nikolic to see how the purchase of raspberries was unfolding." So understand your testimony, you're at Kravica on the night of the 13th, confronted by a policeman with a gun in fatigues, you're told that Muslims had been murdered in the warehouse, you can hear what you believe to be murders ongoing, and the next morning you go back to the warehouse because you've got to do a raspberry audit or something?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Among other things that was a reason too. There was the sales point, there was merchandise coming in. I had no information for a day or two, and I had no idea how many victims were inside. We were able to agree with Dragan. We went back there on the 14th and saw an even worse sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And when you were asked a question, this is on page 5 of the English, page 3 of the B/C/S, you stated -- sorry, page 6 of the English, page 4 of the B/C/S, that -- well, I'll have to find it, but you stated that you concluded that on the 14th it was the same group killing men since they wore the same police fatigues as the man you'd seen the night before?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. No. On the following day the uniform was a military uniform with a phantom hat, a balaclava on the head --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the latter part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try to help you because I'll show you the part I'm talking about. It's page 7 of the English, my mistake, Serbian page 4. And I'll read it out to you. "On the Prosecution's question whether the police you saw in front of the warehouse on 14 July was the same police he had registered the previous evening, he states that it was and that he made his conclusion based on the police fatigues in which the policemen were dressed." Right. So when you were speaking under oath -- let me finish my question. When you were speaking under oath to the prosecutor, you said you thought it was the same unit because the uniforms were the same as the man you'd seen the night before; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The unit that had committed the killings, that's the unit I meant. As for the people, there were no more people there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not recorded that the witness in his previous answer said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the accused. Could he please repeat the latter part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not recorded that the witness said that the police officers he had seen on the 13th he did not see again on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Which is contrary to your statement. That's my point. You concluded they were the same because of the uniforms. If that's wrong, just say it's wrong and I'll ask you another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a reference to the line where it says so?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I already gave you the reference, Mr. Karadzic -- I already gave the reference. He should keep up. It's on page 4 of the B/C/S, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I see neither the page number nor apart from that a page of 50 lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. It should be --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe you could point at it with the cursor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It should begin "na pitanje tuzilastva," "on the Prosecution's question."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be read out the following part: "I didn't see that but I could --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, no, no. The witness has the statement in front of him. It's an inappropriate intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, it's not inappropriate for another party to ask that the context of a statement be made available to the witness, so Mr. Nicholls can relax and allow Dr. Karadzic at least to make that request to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if I could respond, I disagree that during my cross-examination that the opposing party can tell me what to read out. That's for redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me take a look. I think sufficient part has been read out to the witness. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, again, if we can go to page 6 -- page 6 of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Print it out, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what did you say, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no I didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Sorry, I -- I made a mistake, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If somebody wants a hard copy, I have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, on page 6 of the English, page 4 of the Serbian, there's a prosecutor's question as to what you found out in conversation with Luka Markovic, and you said that Luka Markovic also confirmed to you that the killings had been committed by the Special Police from Skelani; correct? You said that in your statement to the prosecutor. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You told the state court prosecutor that Luka Markovic told you that the executions had been carried out by the Special Police from Skelani. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I would tender this statement, because it's been adopted largely. It contains information of the witness's whereabouts and what he did on the 13th of July which is not contained in his statement provided by Mr. Karadzic and it also contradicts much of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would not object if there's some particular portion of the statement which contradicts what he said and Mr. Nicholls can point to that, but if there are other things in the statement that Mr. Nicholls would like to elicit, he should do so orally, not to admit a prior statement of a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The entire statement contradicts what the witness said because the statement implies strongly and states - and we can go back over it - that on the 13th of July, he was in Potocari, then he was at work in Bratunac, then he was at home. The statement then goes on to say on the 14th he went to Kravica to see how the raspberries were going, and the clear implication, the plain meaning of the statement to anybody reading it on its own would be that that's the first time he went to Kravica and the first time he learned about the executions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And this statement -- just a second. This statement is only eight pages long?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any difficulty with admitting it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will consult my colleagues. We'll receive it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6201.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic. Did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that the situation with the 13th of July is very clear. July 13 was a workday, and I had no idea what was going on at Kravica. I went to Kravica with three people because we hadn't had any news from Kravica, absolutely none. And it was hard to believe that -- or, rather, it seems hard to believe that raspberries were being harvested during the Srebrenica operation. However, that military operation was going on 30 kilometres from where we were working, and women, children, invalids all were involved in that work. We considered Kravica as a normal area at the time. There was nothing indicating that on 13 and 14 July anything could happen at Kravica, let alone that people could be brought there to be killed. As a -- as a director of the warehouse and the other buildings, I had no such information. I came to the site, and I was confronted by some people. I was informed what was going on. The lights were extinguished and I went home. And on the following day I returned with Dragan, and only then did we find out that there had been many people killed and that those things were going on that we mention in our statements. I do not doubt the events of the 13th of July at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just before we move on from this statement, would you agree with me that there is not one word in your statement to the state court prosecutor that any of the killers you saw at any time were wearing masks?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The mask and these events took place on the 14th. I said here that under special circumstances after being detained or placed in remand prison because of all of this I -- I read all this, but still that's not how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now could you answer my question even though it's obvious, that you didn't not mention the masks in your statement at all, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can't see any mention, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But it's a fact that there were masks and that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Are you aware that Milos Djukanovic gave a statement about this incident?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you are leaving this topic, let me ask a question. Do you have your statement with you, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here? Now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Which you signed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the statement given in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, for -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take a look at the paragraphs 55, 56, and 57. You stated here that you witnessed the killing on the morning of 14th. While your memory was so vivid, why did you tell the Defence that you witnessed those killings on the morning of 14th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I was there on the 14th. That was the following day. I didn't see any killings on the 13th. I did see killings on the 14th when I returned from Bratunac. That's when it was happening. And the statement that I gave in paragraphs 55 through 57 speak about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, back to you Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me just clear this up quickly. You go there on the 13th at night to the Kravica warehouse at about 10.00 p.m.; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then according to you, according to your statement to the state court, you were con fronted by a policeman and Zoran Eric tells you that Muslims had been killed at the warehouse; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was confronted by one policeman, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You answered it.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And he confronted me. He wanted me to go on guard. He mistreated me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You answered the question. You were confronted by one policeman. Zoran Eric who worked at the warehouse told you that night, the 13th of July, that Muslims had been killed, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 24777, please. This is from the Stupar et al judgement in the Bosnian state court which you testified in. It's case number XKR05/24 from July 28, and I want English page 6, B/C/S page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this is the judgement, and they refer to your testimony, on the page in English at the bottom, and on your Serbian version it should be there as well -- as well on the bottom of the page. Yeah. You see your name there "svedok," witness Jovan Nikolic. You stated there -- the judgement says that your testimony in that case was that you arrived at the Kravica farming co-operative on 13 of July after 10.00 p.m. when you heard from Zoran Eric, also a worker at the farm, that Bosniaks were imprisoned there, that a police officer from Skelani had been killed, and that many people who were imprisoned there at dusk that day were killed in the hangar. [As read] "The witness also said that he learned in the days to follow that the captured men who had surrendered in Sandici were killed there. Eric told the witness on that occasion that the Skelani police unit was also there. According to Witness Nikolic, Luka Markovic, one of the workers, told him that a Skelani Platoon unit was in operation that day close to the Kravica facility and that one member of the platoon was killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then if we can turn to page 7 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [As read] "Witness Nikolic returned to the Kravica facility on 14th July, saw a pile of dead bodies inside the hangar. It was that day that the clean-up went on, continued. Witness Nikolic stated to have witnessed the killing of one group of the prisoners on the morning of 14 July. They were lined up in front of the warehouse and killed by the soldiers unfamiliar to him." So you not only said to the state court prosecutor in the statement that we saw what happened on the 13th of July, 1995, you also testified to it the same thing in that trial, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm done with that. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier -- I don't have the page in front of me, that you've always been consistent and told the same story or told the truth. Let me read to you some of your testimony when you were here under oath last time in the Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 2479, e-court pages page 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this is about the people who committed the executions. The question to you was: "All right. Did you ever find out where those individuals were, where they were from, the ones that were committing those executions?" Your answer: "No." Now, when you testified to that -- wait for the question. Wait for the question. When you testified to that for the defence of the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, you lied, didn't you, because you found out immediately that these killers were from Skelani?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. Even then I didn't lie and I'm not lying today either. I testified in the Blagojevic case in 2004. In 2005 I was put in remand prison because of that, and one thing is the statement I gave in remand prison, that is when I was a suspect, and another thing when I gave a statement in this way. There was talk about this police unit but we had no official confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, let me read out another part to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is -- should be e-court page 20. It's T8013.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you were asked again about the executioners. The question was: "Can you describe --" And you said: "I didn't know then nor could I guess afterwards who these people had been. It's a fact what I saw is true." So you again strongly implied to that trial chamber that there was no way you could give any information on which unit had committed these executions, although on the night of the executions and the day after when there were more executions you were told it was the Special Police from Skelani.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, because they insisted and asked me about who these were -- who these men were, what their names were, and the men who committed the killings on the 14th in military uniforms, they were not members of the brigade. Now you're taking this out of context. I don't have that statement of mine, but that's how it was there, and many things that I described are absolutely true, the killings and that I saw them there and that this was the Skelani police unit that was involved, that on the following day the killing continued, but those were not members of the brigade. They weren't men who belonged to anything where there was a command, anyone who commanded them. This was the essence of my testimony in the Blagojevic case. Now, you can pull out of context any documents, but this is the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's go over the context right here, and then I'll go over and you think about if what you said is correct, that the Skelani -- the 2nd the -- Skelani Platoon of the 2nd Sekovici Special Police detachment was not in any kind of command, all right? But for now we'll get to that. Question -- it's not in your language, unfortunately. Question from Mr. Karnavas, a Defence lawyer. "Q. Okay. All right. Now you said when you saw that you reacted, first of all could you please describe to us whether you recognise these individuals? "A. No. "Q. Can you describe -- "A. I didn't know them nor could I guess afterwards who these people had been." Well, you could have guessed these people had been members of the Skelani Platoon since you were told they were Special Police from Skelani.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN NIKOLIC
